**Massed Compute**.

---

The "Memory wall" kept coming up at last week's AI Infra Summit. Here is why it's top of mind

Compute performance has scaled exponentially over the past 10 years, but memory bandwidth has struggled to keep pace. When memory can't supply data fast enough, peak GPU performance goes wasted, which stalls training and inference.

The conference highlighted exciting paths forward, including stacked DRAM and disaggregated inference.

Change happens fast. The optimal GPU architecture today might not be the market leader in 12 months. This is one of the reasons Massed Compute has NO long-term lock-in. Customers stay agile, upgrading hardware without multi-year contract constraints.

Thanks to everyone who connected with our team during the summit.

results.title: Flopper Now Tracks GPU Rental Prices Across 24 Cloud ...
highlights:
# Flopper Now Tracks GPU Rental Prices Across 24 Cloud Providers

337 per-GPU hourly rates from 24 clouds, refreshed every six hours, with price history back to July 2026. The spec database now tells you what each accelerator costs to rent, and who is cheapest today.

Published September 9, 2026 · Flopper.io Research

Flopper.io started as a specification database: peak TFLOPS by precision, memory, bandwidth and power for every datacenter GPU. Specs answer half of the buying question. The other half is price, and that number lives on 24 different pricing pages, in 24 different units. As of today, the pricing index collects 337 live listings from 24 GPU cloud providers, covering 89 GPUs, normalized to one unit: US dollars per GPU per hour. The pipeline refreshes every six hours and has recorded every price change since 14 July 2026, so each GPU page now carries a price history alongside its spec sheet.

## What the Same GPU Costs, Cloud to Cloud

The spread is the story. On the day of publication, an on-demand H100 SXM5 80 GB (2022) is listed by 16 providers, and the most expensive listing costs nearly seven times the cheapest. The B200 (2024) shows the same pattern with a three-fold gap across eight clouds. Some of that gap is real: interconnect, storage, support and region all cost money. Some of it is simply price discovery that has not happened yet, because nobody was lining the numbers up.

| GPU | Providers | Cheapest on-demand | Highest on-demand |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| NVIDIA H100 SXM5 80 GB | 16 | $1.79/hr | $12.29/hr |
| NVIDIA A100 SXM4 80 GB | 11 | $1.40/hr | $4.10/hr |
| NVIDIA L40S 48 GB | 11 | $0.87/hr | $2.25/hr |
| NVIDIA H200 SXM 141 GB | 10 | $2.99/hr | $10.60/hr |
| NVIDIA B200 SXM 180 GB | 8 | $4.09/hr | $14.00/hr |
| NVIDIA B300 SXM 288 GB | 6 | $7.40/hr | $11.19/hr |
| AMD Instinct MI300X 192 GB | 5 | $2.39/hr | $6.00/hr |

On-demand, per-GPU, USD, as recorded on 9 September 2026. Spot, community and reserved listings are excluded from the range. Each GPU links to its live pricing page, which will have moved on by the time you read this.

## The 24 Providers

Coverage spans three kinds of seller. Hyperscale and general clouds publish rate cards: Microsoft Azure, Oracle Cloud, DigitalOcean, OVHcloud, Scaleway and Vultr. AI-first clouds, the neoclouds, sell the dense H100, H200 and Blackwell capacity that training runs need: CoreWeave, Lambda Labs, Nebius, Crusoe, DataCrunch, Hyperstack and their peers. Marketplaces, RunPod and Vast.ai, list third-party hosts and set the floor for most consumer and workstation parts.

| Provider | Live listings | GPUs priced |
| --- | --- | --- |
| RunPod | 78 | 42 |
| Vast.ai | 70 | 70 |
| Microsoft Azure | 25 | 9 |
| DataCrunch | 23 | 12 |
| CoreWeave | 18 | 10 |
| Hyperstack | 16 | 11 |
| DigitalOcean | 15 | 9 |
| Lambda Labs | 14 | 10 |
| Nebius | 12 | 6 |
| AceCloud | 9 | 9 |
| Paperspace | 8 | 6 |
| Massed Compute | 7 | 7 |
| Oracle Cloud (OCI) | 7 | 7 |
| Together AI | 6 | 3 |
| Crusoe | 6 | 6 |
| Scaleway | 5 | 5 |
| EcoHash | 4 | 1 |
| Cudo Compute | 3 | 3 |
| OVHcloud | 3 | 3 |
| Excess Supply | 2 | 2 |
| Denvr Dataworks | 2 | 1 |
| Vultr | 2 | 2 |
| Latitude.sh | 1 | 1 |
| Beyond.pl | 1 | 1 |

A listing is one GPU at one pricing type from one provider. Vast.ai and RunPod count high because their marketplaces publish hosts for consumer GPUs the dedicated clouds do not carry.

## How the Numbers Are Normalized

No two providers quote the same way. One prices an eight-GPU node, another a single accelerator, a third a monthly contract, and Scaleway prices in euros. Every listing goes through the same four steps before it reaches a page.

- Per GPU, per hour, in USD. Node prices are divided by the GPU count. Monthly rates are divided by 730 hours. Non-USD prices are converted at the live exchange rate on the day of the sync.
- Pricing types are kept apart. On-demand (191 listings), spot or preemptible (31), marketplace community hosts (111) and reserved commitments (4) never share a row. The headline cheapest price on each GPU page is always on-demand, so an interruptible instance cannot masquerade as the market rate.
- Every listing maps to one canonical part. A provider's "H100" is matched to the exact variant it sells, SXM5 or PCIe, 80 GB or 94 GB, so a PCIe price never dilutes the SXM figure. Names the matcher cannot place are logged and dropped rather than guessed.
- Bad data is quarantined, not published. A listing that lands far outside its GPU's price band is held back and flagged for review. Median, dispersion and FP8-per-dollar figures on the pricing index are calculated so that a single bad listing cannot move them.

The full method, including which provider feeds are official APIs and which are published rate cards, is on the methodology page. Curated listings from providers who work with Flopper directly sit in the same table but are never overwritten by the automated sync.

## Price History, Not Just a Snapshot

A price comparison that only shows today cannot tell you whether $2.99 for an H200 is a bargain or the new normal. Since 14 July 2026 the pipeline has recorded 2,297 price points across 58 days and 101 GPUs, appending a row every time a listing changes. Each GPU pricing page plots the last 30 days with one line per provider, so you can see who cut, who held, and who quietly raised.

The index also reports a 30-day change per GPU. That figure compares the same providers' listings at both ends of the window, so a new cloud joining coverage registers as more data, not as a price move.

...

- The pricing index: cheapest live rate per GPU, provider count, median, 30-day change and FP8 TFLOPS per dollar, sortable and filterable.
- Per-GPU pricing pages: every provider's rate for one accelerator, the 30-day history chart, and the sibling variants.
- GPU detail pages: the "Rent" call to action now leads straight to that GPU's live rates.
- Provider pages: each cloud's full price list, regions and pricing models in one place.
- The LLM GPU calculator: size a model, then see what the recommended hardware costs per hour today.

## What It Does Not Cover Yet

Public list prices only. Negotiated enterprise rates, reserved-capacity contracts and volume discounts are not published and are not tracked. Availability is shown where a provider publishes it, and a listed price does not guarantee capacity in the region you need. AWS and Google Cloud are the largest gaps in coverage; both publish pricing in formats that need heavier parsing and validation, and both are next on the list.

Confirm the live rate with the provider before committing. Some outbound links are affiliate links, which fund the pipeline and never change which provider appears cheapest.

results.title: Rental Rates for Older AI Chips Jump 25% as Demand Surges - Seoul Economic Daily
results.author: Seo Ji-hye, Kim Ji-young
highlights:
Vessl AI raised its hourly rate for Nvidia H100 graphics processing units by 24.7% starting this month, following a string of price increases by U.S. neocloud providers such as CoreWeave and Nebius amid a surge in demand for artificial intelligence computing. Supply has tightened not only for the newest chips but also for older models as demand for high-performance GPUs jumps. Other Korean cloud providers also expect to raise GPU rates depending on supply conditions, raising concerns that higher costs of securing GPUs will weigh on service development at Korean AI companies and on government AI transformation, or AX, projects.

Vessl AI on the 1st raised the hourly rate for H100 chips on its VESSL Cloud service to $2.98 from $2.39, according to AI industry sources on the 21st. The neocloud company counts leading Korean AI firms including Upstage and Motif Technologies among its clients and currently operates several thousand GPUs. It has secured about 7,000 GPUs, most of them leased rather than purchased outright. "It is hard to secure the volume we need for H100s — effectively, the price is whatever the seller names," a Vessl AI official said. "As AI demand grows, the number of customers wanting to use GPUs keeps rising, so a price adjustment was unavoidable." The company plans to expand its GPU fleet to about 10,000 units by the end of the year, but intends to keep adjusting rates flexibly to reflect supply conditions and procurement costs.

Other Korean AI cloud companies, including Elice, have also raised prices recently. In the past, rental rates for older AI GPUs fell when new models arrived, but prices for previous-generation chips are now rising as well. Hourly cloud rental rates for the H100 climbed 21.9% over the past month to $3.28 from $2.69, according to Ornn, an AI compute trading platform. That is about 70% of the price of the higher-end H200. Analysts say demand is spilling over to relatively older GPUs because supply of the newest chips cannot keep pace with surging computing demand.

The trend is affecting Korea's AI industry and research community. Some companies have given up bidding for government AX projects because they could not secure the GPUs they needed. Universities and research institutes, unable to obtain GPUs reliably, are scaling back research or searching for new funding programs. "What determines success or failure in business and research now is not just whether you have good AI technology, but whether you can secure the GPUs you need in time," an AI industry official said. "The ability to secure computing resources is becoming a key element of AI competitiveness."

By Thomson Reuters Sep 17, 2026 | 11:16 AM 

Sept 17 (Reuters) – Cloud provider Nebius said on Thursday it will raise pay-as-you-go prices for leasing selected ​Nvidia chips from October 1, ‌marking the company’s second price hike in three months.

Demand for computing capacity to train and run AI models is surging; rival CoreWeave ‌said ​earlier in the ⁠day that it is ⁠signing contracts at higher prices.

Here are some details:

• Rates for selected Nvidia graphics processing units will rise between ​17% and 21%.

• On-demand rates for some central processing units, made ⁠by AMD and Intel, ⁠and memory offerings have also ​been hiked.

• Prices of some CPU-only instances ​will rise by 25% and those ‌of memory offerings by about 41%, the company said.

• The Amsterdam-based neocloud firm said that customers reserving large-scale clusters ⁠for multiple months can receive commitment discounts.

• Nebius’ price increases follow a quarter of rapid ⁠growth ‌in its AI cloud business, ⁠as the company signed four ​customer ‌contracts averaging more than $1 billion ​each.

• Neocloud ⁠firms like Nebius rent out high-powered chips and data center infrastructure needed for AI models.

results.title: AI Compute Is Getting More Expensive: Nebius Raises GPU Prices as CoreWeave Raises $3 Billion | BasisPilot
highlights:
Two very different stock moves on September 17 revealed the same underlying reality about artificial-intelligence infrastructure.

AI compute is in extremely high demand.

It is also extremely expensive to build.

Nebius rose about 4.1% after announcing another round of price increases for cloud computing capacity.

CoreWeave fell about 4.2% after announcing plans to raise $3 billion through convertible senior notes and creating a stock-sale program for up to 35 million shares.

At first glance, those reactions look contradictory.

One AI infrastructure company raised prices and rallied.

Another raised capital and fell.

But together, the moves tell a coherent story.

Customers are willing to pay more for scarce compute.

...

## Nebius Is Raising GPU Prices Again

Nebius said it will raise pay-as-you-go prices for selected Nvidia GPUs beginning October 1.

The company said rates for selected Nvidia graphics processors will increase between 17% and 21%.

Some CPU-only instances will rise by 25%.

Some memory offerings will increase by about 41%.

This is Nebius’s second price increase in three months.

That is a powerful signal.

Companies usually do not raise prices repeatedly unless demand is strong enough to support it.

## Why Demand Is So Strong

AI companies need huge amounts of compute for both training and inference.

Nebius and other neocloud providers rent access to high-powered Nvidia GPUs and the data-center infrastructure required to run them.

Nebius said its recent growth followed a quarter in which it signed four customer contracts averaging more than $1 billion each.

That shows the scale of the demand.

Large AI customers are no longer buying small amounts of cloud capacity.

They are signing multi-year infrastructure commitments worth billions.

...

Nebius’s price increases improve revenue per unit of compute.

That is immediately attractive if costs do not rise just as quickly.

...

The pricing data is positive evidence for Nvidia hardware demand.

If cloud providers can raise rates for access to Nvidia GPUs, it suggests that available capacity remains valuable.

That does not guarantee Nvidia’s own margins or growth rate.

But it argues against the idea that AI infrastructure demand has suddenly collapsed because of recent safety debates.

The market is showing something more complicated: demand remains intense, but the economics of supplying that demand are capital heavy.

...

Higher compute prices increase the cost of training and running models.

Large technology companies can absorb those costs more easily than startups.

That could increase industry concentration.

It could also encourage customers to sign longer contracts in exchange for discounts.

Nebius already offers commitment discounts for large clusters reserved over multiple months.

That pushes the AI cloud market toward long-term capacity agreements rather than purely on-demand usage.

results.title: The Fed Hiked. AI Compute Got More Expensive.
results.author: Portfolio Armor
highlights:
### Higher rates are pressuring valuations while rising GPU prices signal that demand still exceeds supply.

...

Sep 17, 2026

Two Prices Went Up

The Federal Reserve raised its target range by a quarter point on Wednesday, to 3.75%–4%. On the same day, customers circulated a notice from Nebius Group (NBIS 0.00%↑ ) saying its on-demand prices for NVIDIA (NVDA 0.00%↑) GPUs would rise on October 1st.

The reported increases cover both older and newer chips. The hourly price of an H100 would rise from $3.85 to $4.50, while an H200 would go from $4.50 to $5.40. B200 and B300 prices would rise to $8.50 and $9.50, respectively. Those increases range from about 17% to 21%.

...

$NBIS just raised on-demand pricing for four year old $NVDA H100s... For Nebius, I don't think the revenue gain from these price increases is that big. But it's very bullish seeing older GPUs have longer lives than many expected, and pricing keeping up with that fact. Anyway, I…

$NBIS INCREASE ON-DEMAND GPU RATES EFFECTIVE OCTOBER 1. H100: $3.85 per GPU-hour -> $4.50 H200: $4.50 per GPU-hour -> $5.40 B200: $7.15 per GPU-hour -> $8.50 B300: $7.85 per GPU-hour -> $9.50 AMD EPYC Genoa CPU and memory rates will also increase. Intel Ice Lake CPU pricing

That juxtaposition captures the tension in the AI trade. The price of money is rising, which increases financing costs and reduces the present value of distant profits. The price of compute is rising too, which points to scarcity and pricing power in the infrastructure being built now.

...

The same demand pressure appears elsewhere in the stack. Arm Holdings (ARM 0.00%↑) said demand for its new AGI CPU exceeds $2 billion across its 2027 and 2028 fiscal years, more than twice the amount it had disclosed earlier. Arm also said it had secured the manufacturing capacity needed to support its initial $1 billion opportunity.

Memory remains constrained as well. SK Hynix (SKHY 0.00%↑) said in its latest quarterly results that customer demand exceeded available supply. The company began shipping HBM4 during the second quarter and plans to increase production during the second half of the year.

These signals come from three different layers of the stack: GPU rentals, data-center CPUs and high-bandwidth memory. Together, they describe a market in which customers are still competing for scarce compute.

...

The Fed’s hike puts particular pressure on capital-intensive companies that need to finance new data centers before those facilities generate revenue. A higher cost of capital can reduce equity values even when customer demand remains strong.

...

On-demand GPU prices provide a useful real-time test of the AI buildout. Prices that remain firm while providers add capacity would confirm that new supply is being absorbed. Falling prices and weakening contract demand would signal that capacity is catching up.
